name: Bunk Johnson Collection, Iberia Parish Library
writeup: Bunk Johnson, an early New Orleans jazz trumpeter, made southwest Louisiana his base from the early 1920s and settled in New Iberia. He played with the local Banner Band and taught music in parish schools, and after his trumpet was destroyed in 1932 he relied more on yard work and truck driving. Jazz researchers contacted him in 1939, and the recordings and concerts that followed made him a central figure of the New Orleans revival. He died on July 7, 1949, and is buried in St. Edward's cemetery in town. The parish library's main branch holds the Bunk Johnson Collection of recordings, films, books and taped interviews. The start year is approximate.

name: Marsalis Mansion Motel (site and marker)
writeup: Ellis Marsalis Sr. opened this motel at 110 Shrewsbury Road in 1944, when Black travelers could not stay in downtown New Orleans hotels. Performers, preachers and lecturers booked in the city lodged here instead; Ray Charles and Nat King Cole were among the guests, as were Martin Luther King Jr. and Thurgood Marshall. The motel added a restaurant and a swimming pool and closed in 1986. Marsalis, who also worked to register Black voters, was the father of pianist Ellis Marsalis Jr. and the grandfather of Branford, Wynton, Delfeayo and Jason. The point marks the Jefferson Parish historical marker on River Road, near the former site, dedicated in January 2015.

name: Old South Jamboree
writeup: Walker businessman Lester Hodges built the Old South Jamboree on Florida Boulevard and opened it for shows in the mid-1960s. It ran much like the Grand Ole Opry, with a house band and a regular cast of local singers, in a hall that held 800 or 900 people; drinking, smoking indoors and dancing were not allowed. George Jones, Tammy Wynette, Merle Haggard, Dolly Parton, Porter Wagoner, Waylon Jennings, Johnny Cash and Glen Campbell are named among the stars who played there. The last show was in March 2020, and in 2025 the storm-damaged building and its land were up for sale. The start year is approximate.

name: Little Walter Marker
writeup: A marker at Lee and Warshauer streets, put up by a Boy Scout troop from Pollock, says Walter Jacobs lived on this spot. Born in Marksville in 1930, Little Walter grew up around Alexandria and began playing harmonica at about eight, the year used here. He left home young, was performing on New Orleans streets at twelve and reached Chicago in 1947, where he joined Muddy Waters's band. He recorded on amplified harmonica from 1951, and his 1952 instrumental Juke opened a long run of rhythm and blues hits. He died in Chicago in 1968 and was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2008.

name: B.B. McKinney Homeplace Marker
writeup: Baylus Benjamin McKinney, gospel songwriter, evangelistic singer and music editor, was born at this spot near Heflin on July 22, 1886. Educated at Mount Lebanon Academy and Louisiana College, he wrote both words and music for 149 gospel hymns and songs, among them The Nail Scarred Hand, Breathe on Me and Wherever He Leads I'll Go. He taught at Southwestern Baptist Theological Seminary's School of Sacred Music from 1919 to 1931, became music editor of the Baptist Sunday School Board in 1935 and led its new Department of Church Music from 1941. He died in 1952. Heflin Baptist Church put up the marker on Louisiana Highway 792.

name: Rufus "Rip" Wimberly Marker
writeup: Blues guitarist and singer Rufus "Rip" Wimberly was born in Arcadia on December 7, 1926, and made Tallulah his home. He learned guitar by ear as a child from relatives and neighbors, and his marker says that as a teenager he worked at a sawmill all day and played pool halls and juke joints at night. In Tallulah he played with the Bits 'N Pieces Blues Band, and he appeared at the New Orleans Jazz and Heritage Festival and the Louisiana Folklife Festival. His album was called Highway 80 Blues; the marker stands on that highway, East Green Street. The Northeast Louisiana Music Trail erected it in 2022, the year used here.

name: "Pee Wee" Whittaker Marker
writeup: Trombonist Leon "Pee Wee" Whittaker was born in Newellton about 1906 into a musical family: his mother could play "most anything" and his grandfather played violin. He learned to read music and to play clarinet, trombone, guitar, string bass and mandolin. Around 1935 he joined F.S. Wolcott's Rabbit Foot Minstrels and toured the Mississippi River country with them for nearly fifteen years. In 1954 he settled in Ferriday, where, his marker says, he joined the band at Haney's Big House. He entered the Hall of Master Folk Artists in 1982, died in 1993 and was among the first inductees of Ferriday's Delta Music Museum in 2002. The marker stands at the town gazebo.

name: Mable John Marker
writeup: Mable John was born in Bastrop on November 3, 1930, the eldest of ten children, and first sang gospel tunes with her siblings while their mother played guitar. The family moved to Arkansas, where her brother Little Willie John was born, and then to Detroit. There she became the first woman on Berry Gordy's Tamla label. She signed with Stax in 1965, and Your Good Thing (Is About to End) reached number six on the rhythm and blues chart in 1966. Her marker adds that she sang with Ray Charles as a Raelette and later became a gospel minister in California. She died in 2022. The start year is her birth.

name: Robert Finley Marker (Bernice Depot Museum)
writeup: Blues and soul singer Robert Finley was born in Winnsboro but has spent most of his life in Bernice, where he worked as a carpenter, played blues in juke joints and sang gospel in churches. He lost his sight at about sixty, which ended his woodworking business and left more time for music. His debut album, Age Don't Mean a Thing, appeared in 2016, the year used here, and later records were made with producer Dan Auerbach in Nashville. He has since headlined festivals in Ireland and France. The Northeast Louisiana Music Trail unveiled his marker in front of the Bernice Depot Museum on September 20, 2025.

name: Acadian Museum of Erath (D.L. Menard exhibit)
writeup: The Acadian Museum, founded in 1990, has a large Cajun music exhibit centered on Erath's own D.L. Menard. Born outside town in 1932, Menard moved into Erath at sixteen, heard live Cajun music for the first time and ordered an eleven-dollar guitar from a catalog. He was soon playing dances with Elias Badeaux and the Louisiana Aces. In 1961, between customers at the service station where he worked, he wrote La Porte d'en Arrière (The Back Door), which earned back its recording cost within days and became a Cajun standard. He later built ash rocking chairs in a shop beside his house and was named a National Heritage Fellow in 1994.

name: Hackberry (home of the Hackberry Ramblers)
writeup: Fiddler Luderin Darbone and multi-instrumentalist Edwin Duhon met in this oil-field village, where their fathers had come to work, and formed the Hackberry Ramblers here in 1933. Having learned the latest country hits from the radio, they mixed Cajun music with country and western swing. They signed with RCA's Bluebird label in 1935 and made an early recording of Jolie Blonde, broadcast live from Lake Charles, and brought amplification to local dance halls by running a Sears public address system off the battery of Darbone's Model T Ford. The band played its last show in November 2005. The point marks the community itself, not a building.
